Compare with an ordinary withdrawal. Taking the same CAD 20,000 as a normal RRSP withdrawal would put it all into income in the withdrawal years, with tax withheld up front, and the RRSP room would not come back; the RRSP withholding guide shows that gap. The LLP spreads any shortfall over ten years, often at a lower rate once the student is working again.
Full-time enrolment is required, unless the student meets a disability condition, in which case part-time works.

Leaving the program or never enrolling. CRA allows a withdrawal to be cancelled, by repaying it to an RRSP of your own, if the student did not enrol in time, or left before April of the year after the withdrawal with at least 75% of tuition refundable. Residents generally must repay by 31 December of the year after the withdrawal; anything not repaid is added to income for the withdrawal year.

Limits: up to CAD 10,000 in a calendar year and CAD 20,000 in total each time you participate. There is no cap on the number of withdrawals, but each needs its own Form RC96. Tax is withheld on any part above the CAD 10,000 annual limit, which is then a normal taxable withdrawal.

New contributions just before withdrawing. A contribution must stay in the RRSP for 90 days before an LLP withdrawal to be fully deductible; part of a contribution made in the 89 days before may not be deductible if the plan’s value after the withdrawal is less than the contribution.

One plan at a time. You can participate again only from the year after your balance reaches zero, and a Home Buyers’ Plan repayment cannot also count as an LLP repayment. The Home Buyers’ Plan guide covers that program’s different schedule.

One-year certificate. CAD 10,000 withdrawn in 2026; the student finishes that year. Repayments of CAD 1,000 start for 2028 and end for 2037. With full repayment, the growth given up by 2037 is about CAD 5,381.

Paying it: contributions to any of your own RRSPs, PRPPs or SPPs made during the repayment year or in the first 60 days of the next year count, once you designate them on Schedule 7 of your return. A repayment is not a contribution, so it is never deductible, and it does not need RRSP room.

Paying less: the shortfall is added to income on line 12900. In CRA’s example, Josée owes CAD 1,000, designates CAD 700, and includes CAD 300 in income. Her next requirement is still CAD 1,000, because the balance falls by the full required amount.

Paying more: an early or extra repayment lowers later amounts. CRA’s Alexander has CAD 8,500 at the start of 2021, repays CAD 850 for three years and then CAD 4,000 in 2024; the 2025 requirement drops to CAD 325, which is CAD 1,950 divided by six years left.

Repayments compete with new saving. They use cash but give no deduction. During the repayment years, an employer RRSP match or an FHSA may deserve the money first; a shortfall is a deliberate, priced choice rather than a disaster.
The education is the return. The calculator prices only the RRSP side. The career retraining payback guide sets the cost of a program against the income it may add.

The program must be a qualifying educational program at a designated institution: post-secondary level (or occupational skills at a certified institution), lasting three consecutive months or more, and requiring at least 10 hours a week of courses or work, not counting study time.

The same program, repaying 70%. If cash is tight and only CAD 1,400 of each CAD 2,000 is designated, CAD 600 a year, CAD 6,000 in all, is added to income. At a 30% marginal rate that is CAD 1,800 of tax spread over ten years. The RRSP ends about CAD 19,206 short of the no-withdrawal path: CAD 6,000 of principal that never came back and CAD 13,206 of lost growth.
The student must be you or your spouse or common-law partner, never a child. You must keep the same student until the year after your LLP balance is back to zero.

Timing: a student who has not yet enrolled needs a written offer, even a conditional one, before March of the year after the withdrawal. Withdrawals can continue until the repayment period starts, or January of the fourth year after the first withdrawal, whichever is earlier. You must be a Canadian resident, and you cannot participate after the year you turn 71.

Turning 71, death and emigration. No repayments are allowed after the year you turn 71, so the remaining balance is added to income in yearly slices. At death the balance is included in income unless a resident surviving spouse elects to take over the repayments with Form RC98. Becoming a non-resident generally makes the balance repayable within 60 days, or taxable.

Two-year program, full repayment (the default). CAD 10,000 withdrawn in 2026 and again in 2027; the student studies in 2026 and 2027. Repayments of CAD 2,000 are due for 2029 through 2038. No tax is ever paid on the CAD 20,000. But by the end of 2038, the two withdrawals would have grown to about CAD 36,815 in the RRSP, while the ten repayments are worth about CAD 25,156: roughly CAD 11,659 of retirement savings given up, even though every dollar was repaid.

What does not count: contributions to a spouse’s RRSP, direct transfers from other registered plans, contributions already deducted for the previous year, and amounts designated as Home Buyers’ Plan repayments for the same year.
A tax-free loan from your own RRSP
All three assume the RRSP would otherwise earn 5% a year, withdrawals at the start of their year, and repayments at the end of each repayment year.

An adult going back to school often has more in an RRSP than in a savings account. A normal RRSP withdrawal is taxable income, and the issuer withholds tax up front, so using retirement savings for tuition can be expensive. The Lifelong Learning Plan (LLP) is the exception. CRA describes it as a way to withdraw from your RRSPs to finance training or education for yourself or your spouse or common-law partner; the amounts are not included in income and the issuer does not withhold tax.

CRA checks each year whether the student was a qualifying student, which in practice means enrolled full time in a qualifying program, for at least three months. Repayment starts in the second of two consecutive years in which the student fails that test, and no later than the fifth year after the first withdrawal. For a first withdrawal in 2026:

CRA’s own examples follow the same pattern: Joseph withdraws in 2024, finishes in 2025, is not a student in 2026 or 2027, and starts repaying in 2027; Sarah withdraws from 2022 and is still a student in 2027, so the cap applies and she starts in 2027. One gap year does not trigger repayment, but two in a row do. The repayment period starts sooner for programs that never reach three consecutive months in a year; CRA treats those separately.

Situations the calculator does not cover

Skipping every repayment adds the whole $20,000 to income, one tenth a year, costing $6,000 of tax at a 30% rate. The tax is the visible cost; the larger one is that the money never returns to the RRSP and loses tax-sheltered growth for good. A shortfall is not a penalty, but it is permanent: the RRSP room used by the original contributions does not come back.

Statistics Canada’s preliminary weighted averages for full-time Canadian undergraduates at public degree-granting institutions, released 2026-09-16. Every provincial average is below the CAD 10,000 annual LLP limit except Nova Scotia (CAD 10,029), New Brunswick (CAD 10,373) and Saskatchewan (CAD 10,167). Tuition excludes compulsory fees, books and living costs, which a household may also need to cover; CRA’s LLP pages set conditions on the student and the program, not on how the withdrawn money is spent. Averages are not a quote for any program, and graduate, college and professional programs can cost much more or less.

The LLP has no interest charge and no tax if you repay on time, so it compares well with a student line of credit charging prime plus a margin. Its cost is the tax-sheltered growth the money would have earned. In the default case, about CAD 11,659 at 5% a year; at 0% the cost would be nothing. Unlike a loan, a missed repayment is never sent to collections: it becomes taxable income, and the RRSP is permanently smaller.

The Lifelong Learning Plan lets you take up to CAD 10,000 a year and CAD 20,000 in total from your RRSP, tax-free, to pay for full-time study by you or your spouse. It is a loan from your own RRSP: repayments start once the student stops studying (at the latest in the fifth year after the first withdrawal) and run for 10 years, at one tenth of the balance a year. A missed repayment is not a penalty, but it is added to income and the money never returns to the RRSP. Even when every dollar is repaid, the growth the withdrawn money would have earned is gone.

The first chart puts the CAD 10,000 annual limit next to Statistics Canada’s preliminary 2026/2027 tuition averages. The national weighted average for a full-time Canadian undergraduate is CAD 8,021; only Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan average more than CAD 10,000. For many undergraduate programs, then, one year’s LLP withdrawal covers tuition but not fees, books or living costs, and a two-year program can use the whole CAD 20,000.

The price is a repayment schedule. You owe the money back to your RRSP over, generally, 10 years, and any amount not repaid when due is added to your income for that year. So the real questions are: how much can you take, when do repayments start, how large is each one, and what happens if you cannot make one? The calculator follows CRA’s rules for each.

The required amount is the LLP balance at the start of the year divided by the years left in the 10-year period. With nothing unusual, that is one tenth of the total withdrawn each year: CAD 2,000 on CAD 20,000, or CAD 1,000 on CAD 10,000.

The second chart draws the balance and required amount for your inputs. CRA sends an LLP Statement of Account with each notice of assessment, showing the balance and the amount due next year; it is the figure to follow, not this estimate.

The third chart shows how the income added and the tax change as you repay less of each requirement. Skipping every repayment on CAD 20,000 adds CAD 2,000 a year to income, CAD 6,000 of tax in total at 30%. The fourth chart shows the growth gap year by year.
